title: The princess and the sad dragon
summary: A princess discovers that the dragon was roaring because he had a thorn in his paw.

scenes.text: In a far-away kingdom, very far away, there were tall towers, a river that crossed the village like a blue snake, and colorful flags that swayed in the wind. There lived Princess Ana. But Ana was no ordinary princess. While the other princesses combed their hair in front of the mirror and drank tea with cookies, Ana ran around with skinned knees, messy hair, a bandage on her elbow, and a red backpack full of strange things: tweezers, gauze, a flashlight, a knife with no blade, a jar of honey, and a notebook for writing down everything she discovered. Ana liked exploring the forest and patching up animal scratches more than going to castle parties. One spring morning, while she was having breakfast with her parents, a huge noise came down from the mountains and startled the whole kingdom: GRRROOOAAAARR! It was a roar so loud that the glass rattled, the plates shook, the cats hid under the beds, and in the stables the horses let out a neigh. The whole village ran for cover, shouting: "the dragon, the dragon!" But Ana didn't hide. She put down her spoon, wiped her mouth on her sleeve, took her red backpack, put on her boots, and went out to investigate. "Something strange is going on," she thought.

Ana walked along the dusty path that climbed up to the mountains, dodging loose stones and saying hello to the flowers she knew by name. She climbed, climbed, climbed, until she reached the highest mountain in the kingdom. There, hidden between gray rocks and thorny bushes, was a dark cave, its entrance open like a huge mouth. Inside, a strange sound could be heard. Ana, who had very sharp ears, listened closely: it wasn't a fierce roar, it was a sob. A dragon crying? Ana wrinkled her nose, intrigued. She pulled the flashlight out of her backpack, turned it on, and went in very carefully. The cave smelled of old smoke and wet earth, and in that huge silence all she could hear were her own footsteps. And then she saw him: a gigantic dragon with shiny green scales, two long horns, folded wings, and a coiled tail. He was lying on the ground, his head resting on his front paws, and down his cheeks rolled two enormous tears, drip, drop. "What's wrong, dragon?" asked Ana without fear, taking one more step. The dragon lifted his eyes, red from so much crying, and let out a sigh. Then he showed her his back paw: there was a thorn stuck deep inside, and the whole paw was swollen and red. It hurt a lot.

"Now I understand everything," said Ana, nodding her head. "You were roaring like that because you were in pain." The dragon nodded, his eyes full of tears. Ana opened her red backpack and pulled out a small, firm pair of tweezers. "Stay still, dragon, I'm going to help you. It will hurt for one second and then it will be over, all right?" The dragon nodded again, trusting, and closed his eyes tight. Ana examined the paw carefully, measured the angle, and took a deep breath. With great care she grabbed the tip of the thorn with the tweezers and, in one firm tug, pulled it out. It was long, almost the size of Ana's finger. The bleeding stopped right away. Ana took the jar of honey out of her backpack and rubbed it on the wound. "Honey heals everything," she explained. Then she wrapped a white bandage around it. The dragon opened his eyes, surprised, and moved his paw. He moved it again. It didn't hurt anymore! For the first time in a long time he showed two rows of white teeth and, out of pure joy, he blew through his nose a bright sparkle. Red and golden sparks flew all through the cave like fireworks. Ana clapped happily and the cave filled with her laughter. "I'm going to call you Sparks," she told him. The dragon roared softly, grateful, and licked her cheek with his warm tongue.

From that day on, Ana and Sparks were the best of friends. Every afternoon, after finishing her castle chores, Ana would run up to the cave with her backpack full of surprises: sometimes a piece of cake, sometimes a book to read to him, sometimes a new ball. The dragon would pick her up gently, seat her on his enormous back among the green scales, and take her flying. They crossed the sky of the whole kingdom, whoooosh! They passed over the red rooftops of the village, over the hills, and over the lakes that reflected them like a mirror. Sparks showed Ana secret places that only dragons know: hidden lagoons with colorful fish, valleys full of rare flowers, and caves with crystals that sparkled. The villagers, who had been afraid of him at first, slowly understood that the dragon had never been bad. He was just suffering. And when someone is suffering, sometimes they shout, sometimes they cry, sometimes they roar. But it's not because they're bad. That spring Ana learned something very important, something she would remember all her life and would later tell her own children: sometimes the loudest roars hide the smallest pains. And it is always, always worth coming closer and asking.
